Abstract—Grid integration of Solar energy positively affects 
energy market due to inexhaustible fuel supply and virtually 
zero emissions. However, inexhaustible renewable fuel supply is 
punctuated by the problem of intermittency. Intermittency 
exacerbates the problem of grid operators to bridge the supply 
and demand gap. Thus, precise output power forecast of grid 
interfaced Photovoltaic (PV) systems is required for economic 
dispatch, market regulation, and stable grid operation. This 
study compares the statistical models of Gaussian Process 
Regression (GPR) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) for solar 
power prediction. The models are trained to predict PV system 
output power against the backdrop of data recorded for 
Abbottabad City, Pakistan. Both the models have been trained, 
validated, and compared with each other for varying irradiance 
and temperature settings. The results depicted that SVM based 
modeling excel in solar power prediction with Root Mean 
Square Error (RMSE) lower than GPR based modeling 
technique. Performance evaluation of models is conducted with 
error metrics of RMSE, Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and 
Mean Square Error (MSE). Moreover, prediction quality is 
qualified based on residual analysis benchmarked by load line 
analysis of PV system in Simulink.
Keywords – Gaussian process; Microgrid; Machine learning; 
Photovoltaic system; Support Vector Machine; Solar Power 
Prediction
I. I NTRODUCTION 
The power output of Photovoltaic Generators (PVGs) is 
intermittent unlike the conventional fossil fuel based power 
plants [1]. The key phenomena influencing PV systems 
performance are earth movements and cloud shading. Earth 
movements are deterministic and hence the PVG output 
power is calculated precisely during clear sky over various 
time scales. However, cloud shading is random process. The 
sudden irradiance variations due to partial shading induce 
PVG output power variations. The grid operators are 
concerned for these variations because the abrupt changes in 
grid interfaced PVG power output will result into grid 
perturbations [2].
The recent smart grid management requires real time 
energy production, incorporating demand variations and 
PVG input variations effectively and efficiently. Thus, 
forecasting the energy produced by PVGs helps in the 
effective and secure grid operation. 72 hours ahead 
forecasting is of great concern for grid interfaced PVGs [3].
The significance of power forecast is driven by 
overwhelming grid requirements, ranging from startup time 
of a conventional power plant to the energy market 
perspective [4]. The PVG output power depends on solar 
irradiance that in turns varies with cloud motion and 
movement of the earth. The grid instability takes place by the 
abrupt variations of input supply from solar plant to grid.
Thus, precise forecast is of key importance. The grid operator 
notices the difference between predicted and generated power 
to timely run the backup generators using an accurate 
forecast. Consequently, the low operation cost along with 
grid reliability is ensured [5],[6]. Numerous techniques are 
proposed in the literature to predict PVG power. Few models 
used exogenous data based on satellite images, sky imager 
information, and nearby installed PV models, while some 
other models used nonexogenous information of location [5].
Forecasting span varies from instants to days. Conversely, 
spatial prediction perspectives are from individual location to 
a district. Prediction span is categorized as short, medium, 
and long duration forecast [7]. An Artificial Neural Network 
(ANN) model based 48 hours ahead PVG output power 
forecasting technique for Italy was recommended in [8]. They 
observed that suggested model forecasts PVG power for 
sunny, partial shading and cloudy day having Root Mean 
Square Error (RMSE) of 12.5, 24, and 36.9 respectively.
Autoregressive Moving Average with exogenous inputs 
(ARMAX) for PV power prediction was employed in [9].
They established that suggested model improves output 
precision. A Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) technique
based PVG output power prediction was implemented in 
[10]. Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS) for 
power prediction of PV system was described in [11]. They 
compared results with additional techniques as well. They 
observed that suggested technique achieved better results 
than other methods for testing and training [11].
The extensive literature ex ists about comparison of
statistical and deterministic techniques for modeling PV 
systems. Nonlinear behavior of PVG cannot be accurately 
modeled by using deterministic method. Five parameter 
deterministic model is compared with Gaussian Process 
Regression (GPR) based technique and superiority of GPR

train Support Vector Machine (SVM) and GPR for PV 
system power prediction. Both the techniques are then 
compared with each other for accuracy. The technique with 
low estimated forecasting error is declared as appropriate for 
output power prediction.
The main contributions of this paper are:
x GPR based statistical modeling of PV system is 
developed by considering weather conditions of 
Abbottabad,Pakistan.System is designed for output 
power prediction of PVG and Maximum Power Point 
(MPP) estimation in ambient weather.
x SVM technique for power prediction of PVG is also 
developed for varying temperature and irradiance 
settings. The model is also formulated for MPP in 
ambient weather settings. 
x Both the statistical models are compared with each other 
for accurate solar power prediction. Moreover, 
performance evaluation of models is conducted with 
error metrics. 
The work is structured as: Section II demonstrates 
statistical techniques of GPR and SVM for output power 
prediction of PV system. The generally used performance 
evaluation indicators are also described. Section III presents 
microgrid architecture, training data description, and 
comparative analysis of GPR and SVM. Finally, conclusion 
and future directions are illustrated in Section IV.
II. M ATERIALS AND METHODS
Artificial intelligence teaches computer to learn a specific 
task independently using data without relying on 
mathematical analysis. Machine learning demonstrates 
computers to acquire from experience. The algorithms 
adaptively learn accurately by increasing training data 
samples. The image and speech recognition, electricity load 
forecasting, and data mining are numerous applications of 
machine learning, categorize as supervised and unsupervised 
learning. Supervised learning predicts future response by 
training input samples. Regression learning estimates 
continuous response, while Classification learning estimates 
categorical output [13]. GPR and SVM techniques of 
supervised learning is used in this paper for PVG output 
power prediction.

III. R ESULTS AND DISCUSSION
The comparison of SVM and GPR based PVG modeling 
is presented here. The model with an appropriate output 
power prediction is qualified as better technique for opted 
climate conditions. RMSE, MBE, and MSE serve as 
prediction quality parameters. Moreover, model reliability is 
established through visual analysis of residual plots of 
respective modeling technique.
A. Microgrid Architecture
The system under observation is a microgrid model 
consisted upon 100kW PVG and 50kW backup diesel 
generator connected to a utility grid, as depicted in Fig. 1. The 
diesel generator serves as a peaker plant to balance supply 
demand variance, after the PVG’s internal power reserve is 
exhausted. Unbalance of supply and demand is reflected by 
the grid frequency deviation. The power demand greater than 
supply results in grid frequency rise from nominal 60Hz, and 
vice versa. Microgrid Control System (MCS) is a centralized 
microgrid control architecture, that supplies PWM for 
suboptimal MPP operation[12]. The suboptimal MPP is 
suggested by either the SVM or GPR model, and is fine-tuned 
based on the unbalance grid frequency. MCS also generates 
inverter control signals to produce three phase grid interfaced 
240V (RMS) voltages. During utility grid faults, MCS 
isolates the microgrid by connecting microgrid islanding 
relay. Finally, in the event of the PVG saturation at 95% of 
MPP operation, MCS activates secondary frequency 
protection layer by triggering the peaker plant.

B. Site Description and Data
The training data for both statistical models are yearly 
irradiance and temperature recorded for Abbottabad, 
Pakistan. During Autumn and Spring, temperature changes 
from mild to warm. However, hot weather is experienced in 
middle of year with cool to mild conditions in Winter time.
Heavy monsoon season in July through September is 
followed by sparse snowfall in the months of December and 
January [16]. Both GPR and SVM is trained for the climate 
data of Abbottabad, Pakistan.
The irradiance data illustrated in Fig. 2 as scatter plot is 
recorded annually in HOMER software. Hours, days, and 
irradiance are depicted on the x,  y, and z axis respectively. 
Fig. 3 presents average temperature per month during 2009-
2017 [17]. Peak temperature is observed in the mid of every 
year. The relation of maximum output power, temperature, 
and irradiance is represented in Fig. 4. The collected data of 
irradiance, temperature, and computed maximum power are 
used to train GPR Matern 5/2 and SVM technique. Maximum 
power output is predicted using trained model for ambient 
irradiance and temperature settings.

Pakistan.

month in 2009-2017.

GPR and SVM based modeling.
C. Model Training
SVM and GPR models are trained for data obtained from 
the load line analysis of a 100kW PVG. The climate 
conditions of Abbottabad, Pakist an are tabulated as training 
inputs or predictors. The maximum power of PVG obtained 
from load line study in Simulink is tabulated as training 
output or response. The 515 predictor samples and respective 
response observations are fe d into Statistics and Machine 
Learning Toolbox of MATLAB. Model for training are SVM 
and GPR Matern 5/2 model. Th e models are anticipated to 
forecast maximum power output as anticipated by the 
respective irradiance and temperature, learnt from training. 
Predicted versus Actual plot in Fig. 5. compares SVM and 
GPR responses with true response. The technique of best 
prediction quality is expected to lie flatly on the diagonal line, 
represented by the true response. Fig. 5. depicts a close 
matching of the two modeling techniques.

response.

of two modeling
